Regulators now treat cyber risk as part of process and functional safety.
Cybersecurity is now part of the operator’s responsibility to prevent major accidents.
Wherever loss of control could cause environmental, safety, or operational harm, cybersecurity now forms part of the preventive safety strategy.

In industrial environments, cyber incidents can have direct physical consequences. They can alter sensor values, manipulate control logic, override alarms, disable safety instrumentation, or enable unauthorized adjustments to equipment. Each of these actions weakens safety barriers and increases the likelihood of loss-of-control scenarios.
Because of this, regulators increasingly treat cyber risk as part of an operator’s duty to prevent major accidents. The principle is clear:
Increasingly include cyber-physical risk analysis as part of operational safety
Regulators expect operators to demonstrate cyber risk management as part of their safety frameworks.
This allows duty-holders to demonstrate that cybersecurity measures form part of their “necessary measures” under Seveso III, COMAH, OSHA PSM, EPA RMP, and other global safety frameworks.
